a few immunoviral mechanisms, as observed in the exotic animal reservoirs, might be responsible for the asymptomatic nature of SARS CoV-2 infection.

Asymptomatic COVID-19 Infection in Children and Adolescents:
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a vast proportion of individuals infected with COVID 19 remain asymptomatic and do not show any symptoms of the disease.

asymptomatic COVID 19 is a consequence of the interplay between the viral pathogenesis and the host immune responses, and the host immune system is able to contain the virus and prevent the development of the disease.
the asymptomatic nature of SARS CoV type 2 infection is not a mere coincidence but is a result of an orchestrated immunological response, which is yet to be fully deciphered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the innate immune sensing of SARS CoV type 2 viral components, particularly viral RNA and viral proteases, in the host cells, and the subsequent induction of interferon (IFN) responses, is the primary determinant for the development of COVID 19 symptoms.
, the unique evolutionary advantage of bats and pangolins, in terms of viral control and inflammatory regulation, could be a key factor for the asymptomatic nature of COVID 19 in humans.
a unique combination of viral and host factors, such as viral replication kinetics, viral tropism, viral virulence factors, and host immune sensing, could determine the outcome of the infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the innate immune response in bats, pangolins, and other exotic animal species may hold the key for developing novel therapeutic strategies against COVID19 infection.

, in addition to the innate and adaptive immune responses, the unique evolutionary advantage of exotic animal reservoirs to remain asymptomatic despite a heavy viral burden may be due to the ability to sense and respond to viral RNA and/or proteins, and to regulate the pro-inflammatory response to prevent the development of disease.

a better understanding of the mechanisms that allow exotic animals to control viral infection and inflammation may help to develop therapeutic strategies against COVID-19 infection in humans, which is the need of the hour.
